breakfast.name: Manakish (Thyme Flatbread)
ingredients: Pizza-style dough (flour, yeast, olive oil, salt)
Za'atar spice mix (dried thyme, sumac, sesame seeds)
instructions: Make the dough — let it rise 1 hour
Stretch into thin rounds — not too thick
Mix za'atar with olive oil into a paste — the ratio is personal, family-specific
Spread za'atar-oil paste generously over the dough
Bake in a very hot oven (250°C) or on a saj (domed griddle) — 5-7 min
The dough blisters, the za'atar oils bloom and become fragrant
Serve folded with tomato and cucumber, or open-faced
Manakish is Lebanon's breakfast — ordered from the bakery every morning
The smell of za'atar baking in olive oil is the smell of Lebanese mornings
Cheese version (manakish bi jibneh) is the other classic — mozzarella-like akkawi
breakfast.description: Lebanon's morning flatbread — dough spread with za'atar-olive oil paste and baked until blistered, eaten folded with tomato and cucumber. Every Lebanese morning starts with manakish from the bakery. The za'atar-in-hot-olive-oil fragrance is the smell of Lebanese mornings.

breakfast.name: Ful Medames wa Hummus (Fava Beans and Chickpea Dip)
instructions: Simmer fava beans with garlic, cumin, lemon juice, olive oil
Mash partially — some whole beans, some mashed
Make hummus: blend chickpeas, tahini, garlic, lemon, salt until silky
The hummus should be very smooth — Lebanese hummus is famously smooth
Both are served warm in shallow dishes, pooled with olive oil
Tear flatbread to scoop both
The combination of ful (earthy, lemony fava) and hummus (creamy chickpea) is breakfast
Ful and hummus platters are Lebanon's shared breakfast — the mezze begins at 7am
The olive oil pool in the center of hummus is the visual signature
Lemon juice and garlic are the two flavors that define Lebanese cooking
breakfast.description: Lebanon's shared breakfast plates — lemony fava beans (ful) alongside silky tahini-rich hummus, both pooled with olive oil and eaten with flatbread. Lebanese hummus is the global standard: smooth, lemony, generous with tahini. The olive oil pool and flatbread-scooping ritual are the start of every Lebanese day.

breakfast.name: Labneh with Olive Oil (Strained Yogurt)
instructions: Strain full-fat yogurt overnight — it becomes thick, almost cream-cheese
Place in a shallow dish
Pour generous olive oil over
Sprinkle za'atar and/or dried mint
Serve with olives, sliced cucumber, tomato
Tear bread and scoop the labneh — the oil-rich creamy tang is addictive
Labneh can be rolled into balls and preserved in olive oil — keeps for weeks
Lebanese labneh is made from the yogurt — the whey drains overnight
The tanginess and the olive oil richness together are the Lebanese flavor
Labneh balls rolled in za'atar or dried chilies are a market staple
breakfast.description: Lebanon's strained yogurt — full-fat yogurt drained overnight until thick and tangy, pooled with olive oil and za'atar. The simplest and most beloved Lebanese morning food. Rolling labneh into olive-oil-preserved balls is a traditional preservation technique that becomes a luxury product.

breakfast.name: Kaak (Lebanese Street Sesame Bread Ring)
instructions: Make a soft yeast dough enriched with olive oil
Shape into rings — the traditional kaak shape
Dip each ring in sesame seeds — both sides, heavily coated
Bake until golden — the sesame should toast on the outside
The sesame-covered ring is crispy outside, soft inside
Some versions have za'atar or anise worked into the dough
Sold from street carts hung on long poles — the vendor carries them stacked
Kaak is Lebanon's grab-and-go breakfast — a sesame ring eaten while walking
The street vendor with rings stacked on their arm is a Beirut icon
The crunch of sesame against the soft anise-scented dough is distinctly Lebanese
breakfast.description: Beirut's street breakfast — sesame-coated bread rings sold from carts, the vendor carrying them stacked on a long pole. The crunch of heavy sesame seeds against soft anise-scented bread while walking to work is one of Beirut's iconic morning rituals. A living piece of Levantine bread culture.

lunch.name: Tabbouleh
ingredients: Flat-leaf parsley (enormous amount — this is the base, not the garnish)
Fine bulgur wheat (a very small amount)
instructions: IMPORTANT: Tabbouleh is primarily parsley — not bulgur — this is the Lebanese truth
Finely chop an entire large bunch of parsley — the knife work is the dish
Dice tomatoes very small — they should bleed into the parsley
Add finely sliced scallions, torn mint
Soak bulgur in lemon juice and tomato juice — it swells gently (no cooking)
Dress generously with lemon juice and olive oil
Allspice is the flavor note that makes Lebanese tabbouleh distinct
The ratio: 80% parsley, 10% bulgur, 10% tomato is correct
Restaurants outside Lebanon make 'tabbouleh' that's mostly bulgur — incorrect
Tabbouleh is Lebanon's most exported dish and most misrepresented abroad
lunch.description: Lebanon's most misrepresented export — tabbouleh is 80% finely chopped parsley with a small amount of bulgur, not the other way around. The lemon juice, allspice, and olive oil dressing and the knife-skill-intensive parsley-chopping are authentic. Every Lebanese family has strong opinions about the ratio.

lunch.name: Fattoush (Bread Salad)
ingredients: Romaine lettuce, tomatoes, cucumber, radish, scallion
Pita bread (toasted or fried until very crispy)
instructions: Toast or fry pita until very crispy — it should crunch loudly
The bread should be distinct, not soggy — add just before serving
Chop all vegetables into similar-sized pieces
Make dressing: lemon juice, olive oil, garlic, sumac, salt
Toss vegetables with dressing
Add crispy pita pieces last — toss quickly to maintain crunch
Sumac provides sourness without liquid — it's the dry sour
The moment the bread hits the salad, a timer starts — eat immediately
Fattoush is Lebanon's anti-waste bread salad — stale pita transformed
The sumac-tart dressing and the crispy-before-soggy pita race are the dish's drama
lunch.description: Lebanon's anti-waste bread salad — stale pita fried to a shard, tossed with vegetables, sumac, and lemon dressing at the last possible moment. A race against sogginess: eat immediately after the pita goes in. The sumac sourness, the fresh herb abundance, and the crispy-to-soggy transformation make fattoush one of Lebanon's most dynamic dishes.

lunch.name: Kibbeh Nayeh (Raw Lamb Kibbeh)
ingredients: Lamb shoulder (very fresh, chilled — high quality essential)
Spiced lamb filling: pine nuts, onion, lamb, allspice (for stuffed version)
instructions: Kibbeh nayeh is raw minced lamb — meat quality and freshness are non-negotiable
Use only very fresh lamb from a trusted butcher
Soak fine bulgur in ice water — it softens without cooking
Mince lamb by hand with a sharp knife or food processor
Mix lamb with bulgur, spices, mint, onion — knead like a dough
The kneading develops a smooth, firm texture
Keep cold throughout — work quickly, serve immediately
Dress with olive oil, serve with fresh mint, green onions, flatbread
Kibbeh nayeh is Lebanon's most prized dish — a delicacy for special guests
The raw lamb trust — the quality judgment — is the Lebanese host's statement of confidence
lunch.description: Lebanon's most prized delicacy — raw minced lamb mixed with bulgur, allspice, and mint, shaped and dressed with olive oil. The host's choice to serve kibbeh nayeh is a statement of confidence in the lamb's quality. A dish requiring trust, freshness, and knife skill — Lebanon's steak tartare.

lunch.name: Hummus bi Tahini
ingredients: Tahini (generous — Lebanese hummus uses a lot)
instructions: Soak chickpeas overnight — 8+ hours
Cook until very soft — 1-1.5 hours (overcooking makes better hummus)
The slightly overdone chickpea blends to a creamier texture
Reserve some cooking liquid
Blend chickpeas with tahini, lemon, garlic, garlic, and ice water — yes, ice water
The ice water creates the unique Lebanese hummus creaminess and lightness
Blend for a full 3-4 minutes — longer than you think necessary
Season generously with salt and lemon
Serve warm with olive oil pool, paprika, cumin
Lebanese hummus is the standard by which all hummus is judged
lunch.description: Lebanon's hummus — the global benchmark. The secrets: dried chickpeas cooked until very soft, generous tahini, ice water blended in for lightness, and a full 3-4 minutes of blending. Served warm with an olive oil pool. Lebanese hummus is creamier, lighter, and more generously tahini-forward than all other versions.

lunch.name: Mezze Platter (Lebanese Spread)
instructions: Lebanese mezze is not a single dish — it is a philosophy of eating
Every dish is set simultaneously on the table — no courses
The table fills until there's no room left — this is correct
Dip, tear, scoop, share — no individual plates
Hummus is the center, the anchor
Baba ganoush pairs with it — smoky eggplant to hummus's earthiness
Stuffed grape leaves (warak dawali) are time-intensive and revered
Kibbeh — fried or baked — is the protein center
The mezze conversation is the real meal — food is the medium
Warak dawali is the most labor-intensive and most prized — each leaf rolled individually
lunch.description: Lebanon's dining philosophy — mezze is not a starter but the entire meal: hummus, baba ganoush, tabbouleh, stuffed grape leaves, kibbeh, and falafel all set simultaneously. The table fills until there's no room. Sharing, tearing, and scooping while talking — the mezze conversation is the real event and food is its medium.

dinner.name: Kafta (Spiced Lamb Kebab)
instructions: Grate onion — the moisture helps the kafta stick together
Mix ground lamb with onion, parsley, spices — by hand until cohesive
The mixture should be sticky and hold its shape
Shape around flat metal skewers — the flat surface grips the meat
Grill over charcoal — the allspice and fat dripping onto coals is the smell
Rotate regularly — 8-10 minutes total
The kafta should be slightly pink inside, charred outside
Serve with flatbread, tomato, and tahini sauce
Kafta is Lebanese everyday grilled meat — the most democratic dish
It's in every home, every street corner, every village grill
dinner.description: Lebanon's everyday grilled meat — spiced lamb mixed with grated onion, parsley, and allspice, shaped on flat skewers and grilled over charcoal. The allspice-cinnamon spice profile and the char from fat dripping onto coals are the Lebanese grill signature. From village backyard to Beirut restaurant, kafta is democratic and perfect.

dinner.name: Sayadieh (Lebanese Fish and Rice)
instructions: Caramelize a very large amount of onions — low heat, 30+ minutes — this is the soul of the dish
The onions go from raw to golden to deep amber — patience
Add cumin, coriander, allspice to the onions
Fry fish separately until golden on both sides — crispy skin
Build the rice: cook with the caramelized onion broth
The onion-tinted broth colors the rice amber
Layer fish over rice for the final 10 minutes of cooking
Garnish with toasted pine nuts, crispy fried onions
Serve with tahini sauce and lemon
Sayadieh is the dish of coastal Lebanon — fishermen's food elevated to celebration
dinner.description: Coastal Lebanon's celebrated fish dish — sea bass over onion-and-spice-perfumed rice, the deep amber color from long-caramelized onions. The caramelized onion broth is the soul of sayadieh — it colors the rice and perfumes every grain. Garnished with toasted pine nuts and served with tahini, it's fishermen's food elevated to feast.

dinner.name: Kibbeh bil Sanieh (Baked Kibbeh)
ingredients: Outer shell: fine bulgur, lamb, onion, allspice
Filling: ground lamb, onions, pine nuts, allspice, cinnamon, butter
instructions: Make the outer kibbeh dough: fine bulgur soaked briefly, mixed with ground lamb, onion, spices
The dough should be smooth and sticky — very cold while working
Make the filling: saute onions until soft, add lamb, spices, pine nuts — cook through
Press half the kibbeh dough into an oiled baking dish — smooth layer
Spread filling evenly across the bottom layer
Cover with remaining kibbeh dough — press firmly to seal
Score the top in diamond patterns with a knife
Drizzle generously with olive oil — the diamonds allow it to penetrate
Bake 40-45 min at 180°C until golden
Kibbeh bil sanieh is Lebanon's Sunday dish — the family baked centerpiece
dinner.description: Lebanon's baked centerpiece — layers of bulgur-lamb dough encasing a spiced lamb and pine nut filling, scored in diamonds, drenched in olive oil, and baked until golden. The diamond scoring and olive oil pooling are the visual signature. Sunday kibbeh bil sanieh is Lebanon's family meal equivalent of roast chicken.

dinner.name: Warak Dawali (Stuffed Grape Leaves)
ingredients: Filling: short-grain rice, ground beef, tomato, onion
Tomatoes and potatoes (for the base layer)
instructions: Blanch fresh grape leaves briefly or rinse jarred ones
Mix filling: rice, ground meat, tomato, onion, allspice, cinnamon, lemon, olive oil
Place a grape leaf vein-side-up on a flat surface
Add a small amount of filling near the stem — resist the urge to overfill
Fold stem end up, fold sides in, roll forward tightly — the tighter the better
Layer a pot with sliced tomatoes and potatoes — they form a bed
Arrange stuffed grape leaves tightly in concentric circles
Add water or stock just to cover, add olive oil and lemon
Weight them with a heavy plate — they must not float or unroll
Simmer 50-60 minutes — they're done when the rice is cooked through
Every grandmother has a different technique — the finger-roll method is debated
dinner.description: Lebanon's labor of love — grape leaves individually rolled around spiced rice and lamb, nestled in a pot and simmered for an hour. The tightness of the roll (it must not unravel), the grandmother's technique debate, and the two-hour investment make warak dawali the most revered dish in Lebanese cooking.

dinner.name: Loubieh bil Zeit (Green Beans in Olive Oil)
ingredients: Fresh green beans (or flat romano beans)
instructions: Heat generous olive oil in a pot
Add sliced onion — saute until soft and golden
Add garlic — cook briefly, fragrant
Add tomatoes — cook until they break down into a sauce
Add green beans — whole or halved
Season with allspice, cinnamon, salt
Simmer 20-25 min until beans are very tender, not crunchy
The olive oil becomes infused with tomato, garlic, and beans
Serve at room temperature — it's better not hot
Loubieh bil zeit is Lebanon's vegetarian staple — part of every mezze
The olive oil enriched tomato sauce and soft beans are deeply satisfying
dinner.description: Lebanon's vegetarian soul food — green beans braised slowly in olive oil with tomatoes, garlic, and allspice until very tender and deeply savory. Always served at room temperature — it's better cold than hot. The olive oil absorbs all the tomato and garlic flavors, becoming the real sauce.

snacks.name: Falafel
ingredients: Parsley, cilantro (fresh — makes them green inside)
instructions: Use only dried, soaked chickpeas — canned chickpeas make dense, greasy falafel
The chickpeas should be raw (soaked but not cooked)
Grind chickpeas with herbs, garlic, spices — the texture is coarse, not smooth
The fresh herbs turn the interior green
Rest the mixture 30 minutes — let the flavors meld
Add baking soda just before frying — creates lightness
Shape into balls or discs
Fry at 175°C — they should be dark mahogany outside, light green inside
The crispy exterior and the herb-green interior are the two-texture goal
Falafel is Lebanon's most exported food — but home falafel is a different level
snacks.description: Lebanon's most exported food — but real falafel bears no resemblance to most versions abroad. Made from raw soaked chickpeas (never canned), fresh parsley and cilantro that turn the interior green, and fried until deeply mahogany. The crispy-green interior two-texture is the authenticity test. Home falafel is a different experience.

snacks.name: Sambousek (Fried Pastry)
ingredients: Filling options: spiced lamb (with pine nuts), cheese (akkawi)
instructions: Make a stiff pastry dough with flour, olive oil, water
Rest 30 minutes
Roll thin, cut into circles
Place filling (lamb or cheese) in center
Fold in half, crimp edges with a fork in decorative pattern — the crimping is craft
Deep fry at 175°C until golden
The pastry should be thin and crispy, not doughy
The crimped edge is both functional (sealing) and aesthetic
Sambousek are Lebanon's party food — made in large batches for celebrations
The lamb and pine nut filling is the most traditional
snacks.description: Lebanon's party pastry — thin dough filled with spiced lamb and pine nuts or cheese, folded and crimped in a decorative pattern, then deep-fried to a crisp. The crimping edge design is both functional and a marker of the maker's skill. Made in large batches for celebrations, they disappear immediately.

snacks.name: Baba Ganoush
instructions: Burn the eggplant directly over a gas flame or under a broiler
The skin should be completely black and charred
This charring is the source of the smoky flavor — the smoke is the dish
The eggplant collapses and softens completely
Peel away all the charred skin — the flesh inside should be silky
Drain excess liquid — it dilutes the flavor
Mash with tahini, lemon, garlic — not too smooth, some texture is correct
Season well — eggplant needs a lot of lemon and salt
Top with olive oil, pomegranate seeds, parsley
Baba ganoush vs. mutabal: Lebanese names differ by region — both are correct
snacks.description: Lebanon's smoky eggplant dip — the eggplant is burned entirely black over an open flame, the smoke absorbed into the collapsing flesh. The char is the dish: without direct flame contact, it's just a mash. Tahini, lemon, and garlic complete it. The pomegranate seed garnish adds sweetness and visual drama.

snacks.name: Kebbeh Makliyeh (Fried Kibbeh Balls)
ingredients: Outer shell: fine bulgur, ground lamb, onion, spices
Filling: minced lamb, onions, pine nuts, allspice, cinnamon
instructions: Prepare kibbeh dough: soak bulgur, mix with raw ground lamb, grated onion, allspice
Work until a smooth, clay-like dough forms — keep it cold
Prepare filling: saute onions, add lamb, pine nuts, spices — cook through and cool
Wet hands, take a ball of kibbeh dough
Hollow it out with a finger — creating a thin shell
Fill with the cooked lamb-pine nut mixture
Seal the opening — form into an oval with pointed ends
The oval torpedo shape is the traditional kibbeh shape
Deep fry at 170°C until deep golden — about 5-6 min
The crust should be crispy, the inside should have the hot filling and the raw-lamb outer cooked through
snacks.description: Lebanon's torpedo-shaped croquette — a shell of raw bulgur-lamb dough encasing a cooked spiced lamb and pine nut filling, formed into a pointed oval and deep-fried. The pointed torpedo shape is Lebanon's most recognized food shape. The crispy shell, the warm spiced filling, and the pine nuts are three textures in one bite.

snacks.name: Manaqeesh bi Jibneh (Cheese Flatbread)
ingredients: Akkawi cheese (or a mix of mozzarella and feta)
instructions: Stretch dough thin
Top with akkawi cheese (a mild white Lebanese cheese, slightly salty)
Sprinkle nigella seeds if desired
Bake on very high heat — the cheese melts into golden patches
The crust should blister, the cheese should bubble and brown slightly
Fold and eat hot — often with fresh tomato and mint stuffed inside
Manakish bi jibneh is Lebanon's other breakfast staple beside za'atar
The akkawi cheese's mild saltiness and the blistered dough are the keys
Every neighborhood bakery (furn) makes them fresh from 6am
The folded-and-eaten-walking form is the Beirut breakfast walk
snacks.description: Lebanon's cheese flatbread morning — akkawi cheese melted on blistered thin dough, folded with fresh tomato and mint and eaten walking. The neighborhood bakery (furn) opens at 6am for exactly this. Akkawi is Lebanon's distinctive white cheese: mild, slightly salty, with a stretch that mozzarella approximates but doesn't match.

desserts.name: Knafeh (Cheese Pastry)
ingredients: Akkawi or nabulsi cheese (soaked to remove salt)
Simple syrup with orange blossom water
Orange food coloring (optional — gives the orange color)
instructions: Soak akkawi or nabulsi cheese in cold water overnight — removes excess salt
The desalting is critical — salty cheese ruins the sweet balance
Melt clarified butter, toss kataifi shredded pastry in it — coat every strand
Layer half the kataifi in a baking pan, press firmly
Layer desalted cheese across the middle
Cover with remaining kataifi, press firmly
Optional: orange food coloring mixed into the top kataifi layer
Bake at 180°C until the bottom is golden and crispy
Immediately flood with cold orange-blossom simple syrup (contrasting temps important)
Flip onto a serving plate — garnish with crushed pistachios
desserts.description: Lebanon's (and the Levant's) greatest pastry — shredded wheat encasing desalted white cheese, baked until crispy, flooded with orange blossom syrup, and flipped to reveal the golden crust. The salt-removal of the cheese, the hot-crispy-meets-cold-syrup contrast, and the pistachio finish are the three essentials. Often debated as being originally from Nablus.

desserts.name: Baklava
ingredients: Simple syrup with rose water or orange blossom water
instructions: Layer phyllo sheets, brushing each with clarified butter
After 5-6 sheets, add a layer of crushed pistachios or walnuts
Continue alternating — butter and nuts and phyllo
Cut into diamonds or squares BEFORE baking — not after
Bake at 175°C until golden — 25-30 minutes
The layers should be distinct and flaky — visible through the cut
Meanwhile, make cold simple syrup with rose or orange blossom water
The cold syrup-hot baklava technique: pour cold syrup on hot baklava — creates crispiness
Let it absorb — do not rush
Lebanese baklava: lighter on sugar, heavier on pistachios than other versions
desserts.description: The Levant's great phyllo pastry — layers of butter-brushed phyllo, crushed pistachios, and sugar syrup. The cold-syrup-on-hot-baklava technique is the crispiness secret. Lebanese baklava is lighter on sugar and more pistachio-forward than other regional versions. Cut before baking so the diamond shapes are clean.

desserts.name: Ma'amoul (Date-Filled Semolina Cookies)
instructions: Mix semolina with butter — work with your hands until sandy
Add rose water, orange blossom water, milk — bring together to a dough
Rest 1 hour — the semolina hydrates and the dough becomes workable
Make filling: date paste or chopped walnuts/pistachios with cinnamon
Roll dough into balls, hollow out with a finger
Fill with date paste, seal carefully
Use a special ma'amoul wooden mold to imprint a pattern — or pinch by hand
Bake at 170°C until barely golden — ma'amoul should be very pale
Dust generously with powdered sugar while still warm
Ma'amoul are made for Eid and Easter — Lebanese holidays mean ma'amoul
desserts.description: Lebanon's holiday cookie — semolina and butter dough filled with date paste or walnuts, pressed in carved wooden molds to create patterns, dusted with powdered sugar. Made for every Eid and Easter. The carved wooden mold (tabe') and the powdered sugar cloud are the visual signature. Each family has inherited molds.

desserts.name: Ashta (Clotted Cream with Honey)
ingredients: Pistachios, dried rose petals for garnish
instructions: Combine milk and cream, heat gently
Add cornstarch dissolved in a little milk to stabilize
Stir continuously until it thickens
Add rose water and orange blossom water — the floral perfume is essential
Pour into small bowls — it sets as it cools
Top with honey and crushed pistachios
Ashta is Lebanon's clotted cream — similar to English clotted cream but floral
Used as a topping for qatayef, knafeh, and eaten alone
The rose water-orange blossom combination is Lebanese dessert's perfume
The thick, slightly rich cream with honey and pistachios is simple, satisfying luxury
desserts.description: Lebanon's floral clotted cream — thickened milk perfumed with rose water and orange blossom, served with honey and pistachios. The rose-orange blossom scent is Lebanon's dessert signature. Used inside stuffed pancakes (qatayef), on top of knafeh, or eaten alone. The fragrant cream and pistachio contrast is pure Levantine luxury.

drinks.name: Arak
instructions: Pour arak into a glass — 1 part arak
Add 2 parts cold water — in this order (water goes in second)
Add ice — in this order (ice goes in last)
The arak turns milky white ('louches') when water hits — the cloud is called 'the milk'
Never add water after ice — it doesn't louche properly
The anise flavor blooms when diluted
Drink slowly — arak is not shot, it's sipped over hours
Arak is paired with mezze — it cuts through rich, fatty foods
'Arak ma ma' — arak with water — is the Lebanese phrase for perfection
Lebanon's arak is among the finest in the world — aged in clay amphoras
drinks.description: Lebanon's national spirit — distilled grape and anise, turned milky white ('the cloud') when water is added. The sequence matters: arak first, water second, ice last, or it won't louche. Sipped slowly over hours with mezze, never shot. Lebanese arak aged in clay amphoras is considered the world's finest.

drinks.name: Jallab (Rose Raisin Drink)
ingredients: Jallab syrup (made from grape juice, rose water, dates)
instructions: Mix jallab syrup with cold water and rose water
Pour over ice in a tall glass
Float pine nuts on the surface — they stay on top
Add a few raisins
The pink-purple drink with floating pine nuts is the visual
Jallab is Lebanon's traditional celebration drink — non-alcoholic
Served at weddings, religious ceremonies, family gatherings
The rose water and grape juice combination is sweet, fragrant, and cooling
Pine nut floaters are non-negotiable — they're the jallab signature
Also popular across the Levant — Syria, Jordan, Palestine
drinks.description: Lebanon's celebration drink — grape-rose-date syrup in cold water with floating pine nuts. The floating pine nuts are the non-negotiable signature. Served at weddings and religious gatherings as the non-alcoholic alternative to arak. The rose-grape sweetness, the fragrance, and the pine nut texture make jallab uniquely Levantine.

drinks.name: Lebanese Coffee (Qahwa Baida)
ingredients: Coffee (light roast — or sometimes no coffee)
instructions: Lebanese coffee is different from Turkish coffee — often lighter, sometimes nearly floral
Boil water with cardamom pods — crushed
Add coffee (light roast) or skip — 'white coffee' is sometimes served without coffee
Add rose water for the qahwa baida (white coffee) version
Pour into small cups without straining — the cardamom settles
Sweeten to taste or serve unsweetened
The cardamom-rose water combination is Lebanon's coffee identity
Lebanese 'white coffee' (with rose water, no coffee) is unique globally
Served after meals, at greetings, at every social occasion
The hospitality message of Lebanese coffee is 'you are welcome here'
drinks.description: Lebanon's hospitality drink — cardamom-scented coffee, sometimes with rose water and sometimes without any coffee at all ('white coffee'). Lebanese qahwa baida (rose water, no coffee) is unique globally. The cardamom and rose fragrance is the Lebanese greeting: you are welcome here.

drinks.name: Lemonade bil Na'na (Mint Lemonade)
instructions: Juice lemons generously
Blend or muddle mint with sugar — break down the mint cells
Combine lemon juice, mint sugar, cold water
The mint and lemon green should be vivid and fresh-smelling
Pour over ice, garnish with mint sprigs
Optional: blend the whole thing for a frothy, green version
Lebanon's mint lemonade is famously refreshing
The Beirut street version is usually blended — bright green, frothy
Lebanese lemon juice is from specific local varieties — more fragrant than average
The mint-lemon pairing is the Levant's classic summer cooling drink
drinks.description: Lebanon's most refreshing street drink — fresh lemon juice blended with mint into a frothy, vivid green cooler. The Beirut street version is blended entirely until frothy and bright green. The Lebanese lemon variety and the fresh mint abundance make this the definitive summer Levantine refresher.
